opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting open questions right now. If you look at how we've been building agents, most of the tool-use capability comes from supervised data: someone writes down examples of calling an API, or we generate synthetic traces, and the model learns to imitate them. That works well for tools that are common and well documented, but it doesn't scale to the long tail. Every company has its own internal APIs, every software environment is a bit different, and tools change constantly. You can't curate demonstrations for all of that.

Think about how a person learns a new piece of software. You don't read the entire manual first. You open it up, poke around, try something, see what happens, and adjust. The environment gives you feedback: an error message, an unexpected output, a result that's close but not quite right. That loop of trying, observing, and refining is incredibly data-efficient, and it's grounded in what the tool actually does rather than what someone wrote about it.

For agents, that feedback signal is really valuable because it's often verifiable. If you call a function and it throws an exception, or a test passes or fails, or the state of the environment changes the way you expected, that's a much cleaner learning signal than a lot of what we get from human preference data. So exploration lets the agent generate its own experience, and the environment's feedback tells it what worked. That combination starts to look like a self-improving loop.

There are real challenges, of course. Exploration has to be efficient, because these environments can be large and you don't want the agent flailing randomly. It has to be safe, because some actions have side effects you can't undo. And you need the model to turn individual experiences into knowledge it can reuse, so it's not rediscovering the same thing every time. Credit assignment over long multi-step trajectories is also still hard.

But I think the direction is right, because it moves us from agents that only know what they were shown to agents that can adapt to new situations on their own. That kind of generalization is what we'll need if we want agents to be useful in the messy, constantly changing environments where real work happens.

r001.rationale: The response describes trying tools, observing feedback, and adapting, but does not frame this as meta-learning or learning how to learn.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify a unified domain-specific language as a representation for exploration.

r003.rationale: The response says exploration can help agents adapt beyond what they were shown, but it does not compare that flexibility with relying on tool knowledge supplied in context.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that when we trained PaLM and later Gemini, we gave the model access to a fixed set of tools, right? A calculator, a code interpreter, a search API. And the model learns to call them because we've shown it a lot of demonstrations of how to use them. That works, but it doesn't scale. Every time a new tool shows up, you need someone to write documentation, curate examples, and often fine-tune. And in the real world, the tool landscape changes constantly. New APIs, new internal services, new software versions.

What's exciting to me is that language models are already pretty good at reading a tool's description or a bit of its interface and forming a hypothesis about how it works. So the question becomes, can the agent just try the tool, see what comes back, and update that hypothesis? If you call an API with the wrong argument format, you get an error message. That error message is a signal. A human engineer would read it, adjust, and try again. There's no reason the model can't do the same thing, especially now that the models are capable enough to reason over that feedback in context.

And there's a second piece, which is that the feedback doesn't have to only live in the context window. If you log those exploration episodes, the successes and the failures, you now have training data that nobody had to hand-label. So you can close the loop. The agent explores, gets feedback from the environment, and that experience improves the next version of the model. That's much closer to how people actually become proficient with a new piece of software. Nobody reads the whole manual. You poke at it.

I'll say the caveat is that exploration is only as good as the feedback. Code and APIs are nice because they give you crisp signals. The harder cases are tools where the output is ambiguous, or where a mistake is costly, and there you need guardrails around what the agent is allowed to try. But for a large class of tools, I think this is the way we get agents that generalize instead of agents that only know what we taught them last quarter.

r001.rationale: The response describes trying tools and updating a hypothesis from feedback, but does not frame this as meta-learning or explicitly communicate learning how to learn.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a unified domain-specific language as a representation for exploration.

r003.rationale: It contrasts exploration and feedback with fixed tool demonstrations and supplied documentation, and says exploration can yield agents that generalize beyond what they were taught.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s promising because an agent won’t always have seen the tools it needs during training. Tools change, interfaces change, and new capabilities become available. So the question is: can the agent learn how to use something by trying it, observing what happens, and adapting?

There’s a useful feedback loop there. The agent takes an action, gets a result or an error, and uses that information to refine its understanding of the tool. It can start with a small experiment before attempting a more complex task.

Of course, exploration needs to happen within appropriate boundaries, particularly when actions have real consequences. But if we can combine that exploration with reliable feedback, agents can become much more adaptable. They can learn to work with new tools instead of depending entirely on examples of tool use that we anticipated ahead of time.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning tools by trying them and adapting from feedback, but does not frame this as meta-learning or learning how to learn.

r002.rationale: It does not identify a unified domain-specific language as a representation for reasoning during exploration.

r003.rationale: It says exploration can help agents adapt to new tools instead of depending entirely on anticipated examples, but does not claim greater flexibility than relying on tool knowledge supplied in context.

sol-6.1.text:
One reason is that we can’t anticipate every tool an agent will encounter or specify exactly how it should use it. If the agent can explore a tool, observe the outcome, and adjust based on feedback, it has a way to learn beyond the examples it saw during training.

And tool use gives you opportunities for fairly concrete feedback. Did the code execute? Did the query return useful information? Did the action move you closer to completing the task? Those signals can help the agent improve its next attempt.

The challenge is making that exploration efficient and safe. You want the agent to learn from mistakes, but also to recognize when an action has consequences and when it needs help. That combination—learning through interaction and knowing the limits of what it can do—is what makes this a promising direction.

r001.rationale: It describes exploring tools and adapting from feedback, but does not frame this as meta-learning or explicitly as learning how to learn.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a unified domain-specific language or another equivalent representation for reasoning during exploration.

r003.rationale: It says interaction can help an agent learn beyond training examples, but does not claim that this yields more flexible models than supplying tool knowledge in context.
